I’m now pulling the full eligibility and covered-criteria sections, plus amendments, so I can give you the actual general eligibility rules rather than search snippets.## General eligibility criteria for CAP/DA services

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2 (Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA))**, NC Medicaid covers CAP/DA when the beneficiary meets both the general Medicaid eligibility rules and the CAP/DA-specific coverage criteria. The policy is **effective September 1, 2025**, and I did **not** find any later amendment changing these criteria. Source: [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

### 1. Basic Medicaid eligibility
The person must:
- be **enrolled in the NC Medicaid Program**; and
- not have **service restrictions due to their eligibility category** that would make them ineligible for CAP/DA services.

Cite: **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 2.1.1 — "General"**. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

### 2. CAP/DA-specific eligibility criteria
NC Medicaid covers CAP/DA when the beneficiary:

- **Meets the required HCBS nursing facility level of care (LOC)** as determined by NC Medicaid, and needs long-term care support at a level typically provided in an institution, related to a documented medical diagnosis and functional care need, **as assessed quarterly**;
- Has a completed CAP assessment showing a **reasonable indication** that the person will need a service plan for at least one CAP/DA HCBS service within **30 calendar days** of the evaluation;
- Has a **signed service plan** authorizing one or more waiver services to be provided monthly, to help prevent institutionalization through coordinated case management;
- Or has a signed service plan authorizing **equipment, modification, or technology** on a short-term basis so the person can return to or remain in their primary private residence and avoid institutional placement; the installation must be completed within **three calendar months** of service plan approval;
- Is **able to maintain health, safety, and well-being** in their primary private residence or another approved location using both **formal and informal supports**;
- Has paid care needs that can be maintained **within the average institutional cost** of the CAP/DA waiver;
- Has a **primary physician** who can link and coordinate all medical services; and
- Has an **emergency back-up and disaster plan** identifying who will provide care if direct care staff are unavailable, the primary caregiver has an emergency, or there is a public health emergency.

Cite: **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.2.1 — "Specific criteria covered by Medicaid"**. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

### 3. General coverage standard
The service also must meet the general Medicaid coverage standard, meaning it must be:
- **individualized, specific, and consistent** with the person’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis;
- able to be **safely furnished**, with no equally effective and more conservative or less costly statewide alternative; and
- not furnished primarily for the **convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider.

Cite: **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.1 — "General Criteria Covered"**. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

### 4. Extra requirements for consumer-directed CAP/DA
If the person wants **consumer-directed services**, they must also:
- understand the rights and responsibilities of directing their own care, shown by completing a **mandatory self-assessment questionnaire** and introductory training/orientation;
- be willing and emotionally capable to assume employer responsibilities, or choose a representative who is willing and capable to direct care;
- have an approved service plan identifying the amount, duration, frequency, and NPI of CAP/DA and non-CAP/DA services;
- receive services consistent with policy and applicable law; and
- sign and follow the **Beneficiary Rights and Responsibilities**.

Cite: **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, Section 3.2.1 — "Specific criteria covered by Medicaid"**. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Plain-language summary
In plain English, a person generally qualifies for **CAP/DA** if they:
- are on **NC Medicaid**,
- need a **nursing-facility level of care**,
- can be safely served at home or in another approved community setting,
- have a **service plan** for CAP/DA services,
- can be served at a cost within the program’s limits,
- have a **doctor** coordinating care, and
- have a workable **backup plan** for emergencies.

## Items/devices specifically **not covered**
NC Medicaid says the following are **not covered** under the Orthotics & Prosthetics policy:

- **Devices for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience** or for the convenience of the beneficiary’s caregiver(s)
- **Backup devices** or **duplicates** kept available at different locations
- **Devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities**
- **Devices or supplies covered by another agency**
- **Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care**, as defined in Subsection 7.3, Coordinating Care

## General criteria that must be met for coverage
For orthotic or prosthetic devices to be covered, NC Medicaid requires that they:

- Be **ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**
- Be **medically necessary** to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s **medical, physical, or functional level**
- Be **appropriate for use in a noninstitutional setting** where normal life activities occur
- Be supported by a **documented face-to-face encounter** with the ordering physician, PA, or NP related to the primary reason for the device, occurring **no more than 6 months before** initiation of the orthotics/prosthetics
- Have the beneficiary’s need for the device **reviewed at least annually** by the ordering physician, PA, or NP

- A **reasonable and medically necessary** part of the beneficiary’s treatment plan
- **Consistent with the beneficiary’s diagnosis and medical condition**, especially the functional limitations and symptoms shown
- **Of high quality**, with replacement parts **available and obtainable**

The policy also distinguishes medical necessity by device type:

- **Orthotic devices** are medically necessary when needed to **correct or prevent skeletal deformities**, **support or align movable body parts**, or **preserve or improve physical function**
- **Prosthetic devices** are medically necessary when they **replace all or part of the function** of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part, and the beneficiary **requires the prosthesis for mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation purposes**

- The beneficiary does **not** meet the **eligibility requirements** in Section 2.0
- The beneficiary does **not** meet the **criteria in Section 3.0**
- The service/device **duplicates** another provider’s procedure, product, or service
- The service/device is **experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial**

I checked the current policy and found **no amendments listed**; the authoritative document is effective **April 15, 2025**. Source: [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment).

## Entrance criteria

A beneficiary meets the **entrance criteria** for outpatient behavioral health services if the policy requirements are met, including:

- **A current DSM-5 diagnosis** (or diagnosis under a subsequent edition of that reference);
- The beneficiary presents **behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment** that are **consistent with and associated with the current diagnosis**;
- If a **higher level of care is indicated but unavailable**, or the beneficiary is **refusing** that service, outpatient services **can be provided until the appropriate level of care is available** or **to support the beneficiary to participate in that higher level of care**;
- The beneficiary is **capable of developing skills to manage symptoms, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapeutic interventions**; and
- There is **no evidence that alternative interventions would be more effective**, based on **North Carolina community practice standards**.  
  **Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 3.2.1.1 — “Entrance Criteria” (effective 2025-04-15): [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## Continued service criteria

For **continued services**, the policy requires:

### First, at least one of these:
- The desired outcome or level of functioning **has not been restored, improved, or sustained** over the timeframe outlined in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary **continues to be at risk for relapse** based on current clinical assessment and history; **or**
- The beneficiary’s gains are **tenuous**.

### And, in addition, at least one of these:
- The beneficiary has **achieved current treatment plan goals**, and **additional goals are indicated** as evidenced by documented symptoms; **or**
- The beneficiary is **making satisfactory progress toward meeting goals** and there is documentation supporting that.  
  **Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 3.2.1.2 — “Continued Service Criteria” (effective 2025-04-15): [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## Discharge criteria

A beneficiary meets **discharge criteria** if **any one** of the following applies:

- The beneficiary’s **level of functioning has improved** with respect to the goals outlined in the treatment plan;
- The beneficiary or **legally responsible person no longer wishes to receive** the services; **or**
- The beneficiary, based on presentation and **failure to show improvement despite modifications in the treatment plan**, **requires a more appropriate best practice or evidence-based treatment modality** based on North Carolina community practice standards.  
  **Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 3.2.1.3 — “Discharge Criteria” (effective 2025-04-15): [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## Related “not covered” limits

The same policy also says outpatient behavioral health is **not covered** in certain situations, including:

- for **sleep therapy for psychiatric disorders**;
- when services are **not provided in person or in accordance with Attachment A**;
- when the beneficiary has a **medical, cognitive, intellectual, or developmental issue** that **would not benefit from outpatient treatment services**;
- when the **focus of treatment does not address the symptoms of the diagnosis**;
- when **Section 5.0 requirements and limitations** are not followed; and
- when the same provider bills **Psychotherapy for Crisis** and **Special Services: After Hours** for the same event.  
  **Citation:** Clinical Coverage Policy 8C, Section 4.2.1.1 — “Outpatient Behavioral Health” (effective 2025-04-15): [8C, Outpatient Behavioral Health Services Provided by Direct-Enrolled Providers](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

In plain language:

- **Start services** when there is a **current DSM diagnosis**, related dysfunction/impairment, and the person is likely to benefit from outpatient treatment.
- **Continue services** when symptoms or relapse risk remain and the person either still needs work on current goals or is progressing and has documented need for further treatment.
- **Discharge** when goals are met enough to improve functioning, the person wants to stop, or outpatient treatment is no longer the right level/modality because the person is not improving.

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
I found the congregate-settings PCS policy, which is likely the key source for assisted living. One more step: I’m pulling the exclusions and comparison policy so I can distinguish congregate-setting PCS from in-home PCS and avoid mixing up 3L with 3L-1.## Short answer

**Yes — NC Medicaid does cover Personal Care Services (PCS) for some beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility,** but the coverage is under **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1**, the congregate-settings PCS policy, **not** the regular in-home PCS policy.

Specifically, Medicaid covers PCS for a beneficiary who **resides in a congregate facility licensed by North Carolina as an Adult Care Home (ACH)** or certain licensed group homes, **if the person also meets the medical/functional criteria and other coverage conditions.** See **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid”** and **Section 3.3 — “Personal Care Services”**: [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).

## What that means in practice

For a beneficiary living in an assisted living-type setting, Medicaid PCS is potentially available if the person:

- has a **medical or mental condition, disability, or cognitive impairment**;
- has sufficient **unmet ADL needs**;
- lives in a qualifying congregate setting, including **“a congregate facility licensed by the State of North Carolina as an Adult Care Home (ACH)”**; and
- meets additional requirements such as physician involvement, no liable third-party payer, and not needing continuous licensed nursing care.

That language appears in **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 3.2.1 — “Specific criteria covered by Medicaid”**: [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).

## Key eligibility details from the policy

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 3.2.1**, the beneficiary must demonstrate unmet needs for at least:

- **three of five qualifying ADLs with limited hands-on assistance**, or
- **two ADLs, one requiring extensive assistance**, or
- **two ADLs, one requiring full dependence-level assistance**

and must reside in:

- **“a congregate facility licensed by the State of North Carolina as an Adult Care Home (ACH)”**, or
- certain licensed group homes.

Same citation: **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 3.2.1**: [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).

## What services are covered

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 3.3 — “Personal Care Services,”** Medicaid covers PCS that occurs at least once per week, including:

- hands-on assistance with qualifying ADLs;
- related cueing/prompting/guiding when part of hands-on ADL assistance;
- certain home-management IADLs directly related to qualifying ADLs and essential to care at the private residence;
- medication assistance tied to a documented condition or impairment;
- assistance with adaptive/assistive devices and durable medical equipment linked to qualifying ADLs; and
- some special assistance/delegated medical monitoring tasks.

Citation: **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 3.3 — “Personal Care Services”**: [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).

## Important exclusions

Even when PCS is covered in an assisted living/ACH setting, Medicaid does **not** cover certain things under this policy, including:

- **room and board**;
- **transportation**;
- **respite care**;
- **financial management**;
- **errands**;
- **companion sitting or leisure activities**;
- **ongoing supervision/monitoring**; and
- skilled nursing or services by other licensed health professionals.

See **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 4.2.1.2 — “Services not covered by Medicaid”**: [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).

## When PCS would not be appropriate in the facility

The policy also says PCS in a licensed congregate facility is not covered when the beneficiary, for example:

- is **ventilator dependent**;
- **requires continuous licensed nursing care**;
- has a physician certification that the placement is no longer appropriate; or
- has needs that cannot be properly met in the licensed care home.

See **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1, Section 4.2.1.1 — “Licensed Congregate Facility”**: [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment).

## Which policy applies — and which one does not

This is one of those topics where the policy numbers are easy to confuse:

- **Policy 3L-1** = **PCS provided in congregate settings**, which is the relevant policy for **assisted living / Adult Care Home** residents.
- **Policy 3L** = **State Plan PCS** generally, and it separately refers to **“Personal Care Services in In-Home Settings”** in its section list, so I would **not** use 3L as the primary policy for an assisted living facility question. See **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L**: [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3l-state-plan-personal-care-services-pcs/download?attachment).

## Amendment status

I checked for amendments to **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1**, and the database did **not** show any direct amendments. So the current authoritative document I’m citing is **Clinical Coverage Policy 3L-1** itself.

## Bottom line

**Yes, NC Medicaid can cover PCS for a beneficiary living in an assisted living facility, if that facility is a qualifying Adult Care Home/congregate setting and the beneficiary meets Policy 3L-1’s functional and medical criteria.**  
**What Medicaid does not cover under this PCS policy is room and board and various non-PCS supports.**

If you want, I can next pull the **monthly hour limits** for PCS in assisted living facilities, or walk through the **assessment/prior approval process** under Policy 3L-1.

Source: **Clinical Coverage Policy 2B-1, Section 5.8 — “Therapeutic Leave”** (effective **2024-08-07**), [Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment). I found **no listed amendments** changing this document.

## Conditions that must be met

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 2B-1, Section 5.8 — “Therapeutic Leave”**, the leave:

- must be **for therapeutic purposes only**;
- must be **ordered by the resident’s attending physician**;
- the **necessity** for the leave must be **documented in the resident’s plan of care**;
- the **therapeutic justification for each instance** must be entered in the **resident’s health record**.

Additional rules in the same section:

- The facility must **reserve the resident’s bed** during the therapeutic leave.
- The facility is **prohibited from deriving any Medicaid revenue** for that resident other than reimbursement for the reserved bed during the absence.
- The facility is reimbursed at its **full current Medicaid bed rate** for a bed reserved due to therapeutic leave.
- The facility **shall not be reimbursed** for therapeutic leave days that **exceed the legal limit**.
- The therapeutic justification is **subject to review** by the State or its agent during on-site medical reviews.
- The facility must keep a **cumulative record** of therapeutic leave days taken by each resident, and therapeutic-leave residents must be marked as such on the **midnight census**.
- Therapeutic leave entitlement **does not apply** when the resident is away **to receive inpatient or nursing services elsewhere, or at a different level of care in the same facility, when those services are paid for by Medicaid**.
- **Ambulance transportation** to the therapeutic leave site is **not reimbursed**, because it is **not considered an emergency**.

## Short answer

- **Annual limit:** **60 days per calendar year**
- **Consecutive-day limit without approval:** **15 days**
- **Core requirements:** therapeutic purpose, physician order, documentation in the plan of care, and therapeutic justification in the health record
